questions.problem:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=4,$ $y=-1,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=({x}^{2}+y)\,i-yz\,j+4xz\,k,$ the flux of $F$ across $S$ can be written as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-yz)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4xz) \\  & =2x-z+4x \\  & =6x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}(6x-z)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,6x-z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071461/assets/581ac462bfcfead22a6c5ad4eb247f05adb1a677e92cac51954b0746cd083ab7.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨x-y,\,y+z,\,2x-3z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by the bounding region of a right circular cylinder of height $3$ whose base is a circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown above. Given that $S$ is positively (outward) oriented, use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $F$ through $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y+z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2x-3z) \\  & =1+1+(-3) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid cylinder enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}-1\,\text{d}V \\  & =-{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =-\text{Volume}(R) \\  & =-\pi \cdot {2}^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =-12\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,j+(x+y)\,k,$ find the flux of $F$ across $S.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z+0+0 \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot [\operatorname{sin}⁡z]_{z=0}^{z=\pi /2} \\  & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}4xy\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}4xy\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (4-1)\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing the Flux Across a Closed Surface as a Triple Integral
canonical_examples.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the finite solid region enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ and the surfaces $z=y$ and $z=1+x^2+y^2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F} = (x+z )\, \mathbf{i} + yz \, \mathbf{j} + x^2y \, \mathbf{k},$ express the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ as a triple integral, and then as a repeated integral.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y) \\  & =1+z+0 \\  & =z+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iiint\limits_R (z+1) \: \textrm{d}V,
$$

where $R$ is a type I solid region that can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \:-1 \leq x \leq 1, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \: y \leq z \leq 1+x^2+y^2 \big\}.
$$

Expressing our triple integral as a repeated integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z+1\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,z+1\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across the Surface of a Known Solid
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the positively oriented surface $S$ given by $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4$ and the vector field $\mathbf{F} = 2x \, \mathbf{i} + y \, \mathbf{j} + 4 \, \mathbf{k}.$ Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4) \\  & =2+1+0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid sphere of radius $2$ enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}3\,\text{d}V \\  & =3{∭}_{R}\,\text{d}V \\  & =3\cdot \text{Volume}(R) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =32\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across a Closed Surface
canonical_examples.problem: Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $y=0,$ $y=2,$ $z=1,$ $z=2.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F} =e^z \, \mathbf{i} + x^2y^2 \, \mathbf{j} + 4x^2yz \, \mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
\iint\limits_{S} \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}
= \iiint\limits_R \textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F} \: \textrm{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{x}^{2}yz) \\  & =0+2{x}^{2}y+4{x}^{2}y \\  & =6{x}^{2}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}6{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=0}^{x=1}\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=2}\cdot (2-1) \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (4-0)\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
